hints: Think about where the fast-moving charged particles come from in an X-ray tube and what makes them move so fast.
Think about what those fast electrons are made to crash into, and why a heavy metal target is used.
Think about what happens to the kinetic energy of an electron when it is suddenly slowed down close to a nucleus.
walkthrough:
**Start with a source of electrons**
You need a beam of very energetic electrons first. A filament is heated by a current, so electrons boil off by thermionic emission. This gives you free electrons to work with.

**Accelerate the electrons to high energy**
A large potential difference is applied between the filament (cathode) and a metal target (anode). The field does work $W = qV$ on each electron, so each electron gains kinetic energy $E_k = eV$ and hits the target at very high speed.

**Convert kinetic energy to X-rays at the target**
When the fast electrons enter the metal target they pass close to nuclei and are strongly decelerated by electrostatic attraction. The lost kinetic energy is emitted as a photon of X-ray radiation, called bremsstrahlung or braking radiation.

Final answer: Electrons are emitted from a heated filament and accelerated by a high p.d. to a metal target. On striking the target the electrons are rapidly decelerated, and their kinetic energy is converted into X-ray photons.

hints: A single X-ray is only a flat shadow. Think about how you could build up a full 3D view from many flat views.
walkthrough:
**From slices to a volume**
In CT the X-ray tube rotates and takes many thin slice images through the body. A computer stacks and combines all these 2D sections to reconstruct a detailed 3D image, so internal structures can be viewed from any angle.
Final answer: Images of the multiple sections are combined by computer to form a 3D image of the body.

hints: Look at Fig. 9.1 for the ray that reaches point P. Which material does it pass through only, and over what total thickness?
Recall how transmitted intensity falls off exponentially with thickness, and be careful to keep $x$ in cm to match $\mu$ in $\text{cm}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
**Identify the path to P**
The ray that arrives at P goes through soft tissue only. From Fig. 9.1 the total thickness is $x = 5.6\text{ cm}$ and for soft tissue $\mu = 0.89\text{ cm}^{-1}$.

**Apply exponential attenuation**
X-ray intensity is attenuated as: $$I = I_0 \exp(-\mu x)$$ Substitute the values: $$I = I_0 \exp(-0.89 \times 5.6)$$ $$I = I_0 \exp(-4.984) \approx 6.8 \times 10^{-3} I_0$$ So only about 0.7% gets through.
Final answer: $I = I_0 \exp(-\mu x) = I_0 \exp(-0.89 \times 5.6) = 6.8 \times 10^{-3} I_0$.

hints: Look at the ray that reaches point Q. It passes through two different materials in series, so think about how to split the total 5.6 cm into bone thickness and remaining soft tissue thickness.
Think about how to combine two successive exponential reductions into one calculation for the final intensity.
walkthrough:
**Split the path to Q**
The ray to Q passes through bone of thickness $x_b = 2.4\text{ cm}$ with $\mu_b = 3.4\text{ cm}^{-1}$, plus soft tissue for the rest of the width: $$x_s = 5.6 - 2.4 = 3.2\text{ cm}$$ with $\mu_s = 0.89\text{ cm}^{-1}$.

**Multiply the two attenuations**
Attenuation happens in series, so you multiply the factors: $$I = I_0 \exp(-\mu_b x_b) \times \exp(-\mu_s x_s)$$ $$I = I_0 \exp(-3.4 \times 2.4) \times \exp(-0.89 \times 3.2)$$ $$I = I_0 \exp(-8.16) \times \exp(-2.848) \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-5} I_0$$ Bone absorbs far more strongly, so the transmitted intensity is about 400 times smaller than at P.

hints: Compare your two numbers from (b) - a large fractional difference in detected intensity means one area looks much brighter than the other.
walkthrough:
**Link intensity difference to contrast**
Good contrast means a clear difference between light and dark areas on the detector. Here $I_P \approx 6.8 \times 10^{-3}I_0$ while $I_Q \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-5}I_0$, so $I_P$ is roughly 400 times $I_Q$. That very large relative difference is easily detected, so bone stands out sharply against soft tissue.
Final answer: Yes, good contrast because the intensity at P ($6.8 \times 10^{-3}I_0$) is much larger than at Q ($1.7 \times 10^{-5}I_0$), giving a large detectable difference.
